text: Where does the carbon released by human activity actually go? Answering that question requires following it through a network of connected reservoirs rather than imagining that it disappears once it leaves a smokestack or exhaust pipe. Carbon circulates naturally among living organisms, soils, oceans, the atmosphere, and rocks deep underground. Plants absorb carbon dioxide from the air; organisms consume carbon-containing material; respiration and decay return much of it to the atmosphere. When living things die, most of their stored carbon eventually re-enters the active cycle and can be absorbed by new plant growth. Some carbon follows a much slower path. Over millions of years, material from ancient forests and marine organisms becomes rock or is transformed into coal, oil, and natural gas. These processes place carbon in long-term geological storage. Volcanoes return a portion of that carbon to the atmosphere. Human beings now release ancient carbon far more rapidly by burning fossil fuels. Each year, humanity emits roughly sixty times more carbon than all of Earth’s volcanoes combined, rapidly transferring material from geological storage into the active atmosphere–ocean system.

text: This paper presents a millimeter-scale 64 × 64 CMOS single-particle radiation detector for external-beam cancer radiotherapy. The device is designed to measure individual charged particles at fine spatial resolution while remaining compact enough for practical integration. Each 1 × 1 μm² diode senses the energy deposited by a single charged particle within its depletion region, and the complete array spans an active area of 512 × 512 μm². Rather than measuring the radiation-induced voltage drop directly, the system records pulse width, defined as the time required for the voltage to return to baseline. text: We examine the phenomenology of a hypercharge-zero SU(2) scalar triplet motivated by two-step electroweak symmetry breaking. Two scenarios are considered: a stable triplet contributing to the dark-matter abundance and an unstable triplet decaying through mixing with the Standard Model Higgs boson. The stability assumption determines both the expected experimental signature and the relevant parameter constraints. The stable case is tested by LHC disappearing-track searches and direct-detection experiments, whereas the unstable case is constrained by existing multilepton collider analyses. Together, these searches probe long-lived charged states, dark-matter scattering, and visible decay products. We find that direct-detection limits exclude a two-step electroweak phase transition involving a stable triplet with a negative quadratic term.
